entries.title: Holding hollandaise and warm emulsions
entries.say: As it reads: holding hollandaise, HOL-un-dayz, and warm emulsions.
entries.summary: How a kitchen keeps hollandaise, béarnaise and beurre blanc warm enough to stay smooth and cool enough not to scramble or split, and the written time limit, labels and clean containers that keep a warm egg and butter sauce fit to serve.
entries.guest: Our hollandaise is a warm sauce of egg yolk and butter, sharpened with lemon. If you have a question about the eggs in it, I will ask the kitchen for you.

paras: Hollandaise, béarnaise and beurre blanc are warm emulsions: tiny droplets of butterfat held apart in a little water, by egg yolk in the first two and by the butter's own milk solids in beurre blanc. Too hot and the yolk sets into curds or the butter oils out; too cool and the sauce thickens, then splits. So a warm emulsion is held in a bain-marie, a pan of hot, never boiling water in which containers of sauce stand to keep warm.

That gentle warmth suits bacteria too. Egg and butter feed them well, and the FDA Food Code sets 57°C (135°F) as the line for holding hot food. A hollandaise in a steady bain-marie can sit at or a little above that line, as the hollandaise entry teaches; a beurre blanc, or a sauce at the bain-marie's cool edge or checked too rarely, slips below it. Below the line the sauce is in the danger zone, so a kitchen with a written procedure holds it on time instead.

Make the sauce in small batches timed to service, each in a clean, dry container, never one that held the last batch. Stand it in water that steams but never bubbles, away from the flame, and stir it now and then so no skin forms. Label it as soon as it is filled, with the time it was made and the time it must be gone.

Check it with a probe thermometer. A sauce holding at 57°C (135°F) or above is hot held like any hot food. A beurre blanc rarely holds that hot without oiling out, and a hollandaise drifts below it as the bain-marie cools, so many kitchens run every warm emulsion on time as a public health control, an exception the Food Code allows only with written procedures kept in the kitchen.

The clock starts when the food leaves temperature control: for a hollandaise, when the yolks come out of the fridge, not when the sauce is finished. The container is marked with the time 4 hours on, and the sauce is served or discarded by then. No time on it, or past its time, and it goes in the bin.

Never top up old sauce with new: the fresh sauce takes on the old one's time and whatever has grown in it, and the label stops telling the truth. Start a new, labelled container and let the old one go.

Pasteurised yolks, heated gently to destroy Salmonella without cooking them, lower the risk from the egg itself, and many kitchens use them for warm egg sauces. Bacteria that arrive later, on a spoon or a hand, can still grow, so the time limit and labels still apply. Whether a kitchen must use them, and how it holds and times its sauces, is set by its written procedure and the local health code: ask the chef.

Beurre blanc has no yolk but is just as fussy: too hot and the butterfat separates, too cool and it sets solid. It holds best at a gentle warmth, often below 57°C (135°F), so it gets the same small batch, clean container, label and time limit. Clarified butter, butter with its water and milk solids taken out, is nearly pure fat and gives bacteria far less to work with, but it is still kept covered, labelled, ladled with a clean spoon and never topped up.

A sauce goes when it has split, turned grainy, grown a skin or crust, smells sour or wrong, or passed its time. One that has just begun to split can sometimes be brought back, as the entry on breaking and rescuing shows, but it keeps its original time.

At Brennan's, hollandaise is the rich, lemony layer over the egg on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, and a preserved lemon beurre blanc dresses the Redfish Véronique. The house notes on hollandaise say what every cook learns: too hot and it scrambles, too cool and it splits. How the line holds and times each sauce is the chef's to explain at lineup.

A guest may ask about the egg. Describe the sauce: warm egg yolk and butter, sharpened with lemon, whisked over gentle heat but not cooked firm. Questions about raw egg, pasteurised yolks or risk go to the kitchen, and the server brings back its answer. A sauce that looks split or skinned on the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, goes back.

cards.front: Why is holding a hollandaise a balancing act?
cards.back: Too hot and the yolk scrambles or the butter oils out; too cool and it thickens and splits. And the warmth that keeps it smooth also suits bacteria.

cards.front: What is a bain-marie, and how hot is its water for a warm emulsion?
cards.back: A pan of hot water in which containers of sauce stand to keep warm. For a warm emulsion the water steams but never bubbles, away from direct flame.

cards.front: Why do many kitchens hold hollandaise on a clock rather than trusting the bain-marie?
cards.back: Water that steams but never bubbles often leaves the sauce below 57°C (135°F), the Food Code's hot holding line, so it sits in the danger zone and runs on a written time limit.

cards.front: What does time as a public health control ask of a warm sauce held below hot holding?
cards.back: Written procedures kept in the kitchen, a clock that starts when the yolks leave the fridge, a mark showing the time 4 hours on, and service or discard within those 4 hours.

cards.front: Why is old hollandaise never topped up with a fresh batch?
cards.back: The new sauce takes on the old one's time and bacteria, and the label stops telling the truth. Start a clean container instead.

cards.front: What goes on the label of every batch of warm sauce?
cards.back: The time it was made and the time it must be gone, written the moment the clean container is filled.

cards.front: What happens to a container of warm sauce with no time on it?
cards.back: It is discarded: without a time nobody can show it is within its limit, and the Food Code's time rule sends unmarked food to the bin.

cards.front: Do pasteurised yolks remove the need for a time limit?
cards.back: No. They lower the risk from the egg itself, but bacteria arriving later on a spoon or a hand can still grow in a warm sauce.

cards.front: Why does beurre blanc get the same holding care as hollandaise?
cards.back: It is a warm butter emulsion that holds only at a gentle warmth, often below 57°C (135°F), so it needs a clean container, a label and a time limit.

cards.front: Name the signs that a held warm sauce must be thrown away.
cards.back: Split into oil and liquid, grainy, skinned or crusted, a sour smell, no label, or past its time.

cards.back: No. A rescued sauce keeps its original time and is discarded when that time runs out.

entries.title: Eggs and safety
entries.say: As it reads: eggs and safety.
entries.summary: Why a runny yolk or a raw-egg sauce carries a risk of Salmonella, who it matters to most, and the habits that manage it: cold storage, clean hands, pasteurised eggs where the kitchen chooses them, and the menu's consumer advisory.
entries.guest: Our poached eggs come soft, so the yolk runs into the sauce. If you would like yours firmer, or have a question about the eggs, I will ask the kitchen.

paras: Eggs can carry Salmonella, a bacterium that causes food poisoning. It can sit on the shell, and it can be inside an egg that looks, smells and tastes normal, because a hen can pass it into the egg before the shell forms. Heat kills it. A firm-cooked egg carries very little risk. A runny yolk, a soft poached egg or a raw-egg sauce such as mayonnaise carries some, because part of the egg never gets hot enough; hollandaise yolks are warmed to a ribbon, not cooked firm.

The illness can be serious for the very young, older people, anyone who is pregnant and anyone whose immune system is weakened by illness or treatment. That is why menus carry a warning, why many kitchens buy pasteurised eggs, and why the safety question always goes to the kitchen.

Eggs arrive cold and stay cold. The FDA Food Code, the model behind most American health codes, asks for raw shell eggs to be stored in refrigeration that keeps the air at 7°C (45°F) or less, and most kitchens simply keep them in the walk-in, the kitchen's cold room, with other chilled food at 5°C (41°F) or less. Keep them in their carton, on a shelf below anything ready to eat, and rotate them so the oldest are used first.

Check every egg as you use it. A cracked or dirty egg is discarded, because the shell is the egg's first defence. Crack eggs on a flat surface, keep shell out of the food, and wash your hands at the hand sink, with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds, after handling raw shells and before touching anything ready to eat, such as toast. Crack eggs as each order comes rather than breaking a big batch into one bowl and leaving it out: one bad egg in a pooled bowl spreads to every portion.

Kitchens that poach ahead slide the cooked eggs into iced water, keep it at 5°C (41°F) or below with fresh ice, and reheat each egg briefly in hot water at service; a tray left to warm on the station goes in the bin.

For an egg broken to a guest's order and served at once, the Food Code's cooking figure is 63°C (145°F) for 15 seconds, and a firm-cooked egg reaches it. A soft poached egg or a sunny side up egg, fried on one side only, is served runny on purpose, and its centre may never reach that figure, which is why such a dish is served under a consumer advisory. Eggs cooked ahead and held hot, such as a batch of scrambled eggs, take a higher figure: 68°C (155°F) for 17 seconds.

Pasteurised eggs lower the risk before cooking starts. Pasteurised shell eggs are heated gently in their shells, in warm water, enough to destroy Salmonella without cooking them; pasteurised yolks come liquid, in cartons. Where the kitchen chooses them, they can go into poached eggs, hollandaise and mayonnaise. Which eggs a dish uses, and whether it still carries the advisory mark, is the kitchen's answer.

The advisory, taught in full under cooking temperatures, marks a dish with a runny yolk, or a sauce of yolks never cooked firm, on the menu and ties it to a reminder, in wording the kitchen keeps, such as the 2022 Food Code's: “Consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish, or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness.” Learn the wording the house prints.

At Brennan's the poached eggs on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Sardou come soft unless the guest asks otherwise, and the house guide says to check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs. The Egg Any Style side is one egg, cooked as the guest asks: confirm the style and doneness as you write it, as the service note asks, and confirm at lineup the styles the kitchen offers.

A server describes how the egg is cooked and lets the kitchen answer the safety question. If a guest asks whether a runny yolk is all right to eat, or a risk in pregnancy, do not reassure and do not lecture. Point to the menu's advisory where it carries one, and offer to ask the kitchen, which can say whether the egg can be cooked firmer or made with pasteurised eggs.
A guest's allergy to egg is a different conversation, taught under the allergen conversation, and it always goes to the kitchen.

entries.title: Raw and cooked oysters
entries.say: As it reads: raw and cooked oysters.
entries.summary: Why a raw Gulf oyster carries a rare but serious risk from Vibrio vulnificus, who it matters to most, the warnings Louisiana and the menu require, the shellstock tags, and how cooking and cold, careful handling change the picture.
entries.guest: These oysters are served raw. As the menu notes, raw oysters carry a risk of illness, more so with certain health conditions, and I am glad to ask the kitchen any question.

paras: An oyster feeds by filtering seawater, and it is eaten whole, often raw, so whatever lives in that water comes to the table with it. In the warm, brackish water of the Gulf, part salt and part fresh, the concern is Vibrio vulnificus, a bacterium that lives there naturally. It is not a sign of dirty water, and an oyster carrying it looks, smells and tastes like any other. It grows most in warm water, so the risk rises in the warm months.

Illness is rare, but for some people it is serious and can be life-threatening once it reaches the blood. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists those most at risk: people with liver disease, diabetes, cancer or HIV, people whose immune system is weakened, and people who take medicine to lower stomach acid or have had recent stomach surgery. Hot sauce, lemon, a strong drink and the vinegar in a mignonette, the sharp shallot sauce served with raw oysters, do not kill it.

Two notices go with a raw oyster. The first is the menu's consumer advisory, from the FDA Food Code: the dish described as raw or marked with an asterisk, and a reminder that raw or undercooked food may increase the risk of foodborne illness. The second is Louisiana's raw oyster warning, required by the state sanitary code wherever raw oysters are sold or served, on a sign, the menu or a table tent. One permitted wording tells anyone with chronic illness of the liver, stomach or blood, or other immune disorders, to eat oysters fully cooked; the other warns more generally of foodborne illness from raw or undercooked food. The manager confirms which the house displays.

Cooking changes the picture. Heat kills Vibrio, so an oyster cooked right through, in an Oysters Rockefeller, a barbecue sauce or a gumbo, carries less risk than a raw one; the Food Code's cooking figure for fish, a word it uses for oysters too, is 63°C (145°F) for 15 seconds. Some kitchens choose post-harvest processed oysters for raw service, treated by high pressure, quick freezing or gentle heat to bring Vibrio down to very low levels while the oyster still eats raw.

Live oysters in the shell are called shellstock, and each sack or box arrives with a tag naming the shipper and its certification number, the harvest area and the harvest date. The tag stays with its container until the last oyster is gone, takes the date of that last one, and is then filed in date order and kept for 90 days. If a guest falls ill, the tag leads the health department back to the water. Oysters from different tags are not mixed before they are ordered, so every oyster can still be traced.

Oysters must stay alive and cold until shucked, opened with a knife for service. Keep them in the walk-in at 5°C (41°F) or less, the Food Code's figure for cold food, in their sack or box, or cup side down under a damp cloth; never sealed airtight in plastic, never in fresh water or melted ice, which kills them. Before opening, check that each shell is closed, or closes when tapped, and is not cracked. An oyster that gapes and will not close is dead and is discarded, as is any with an off smell.

entries.title: Cooling stocks and sauces
entries.say: As it reads: cooling stocks and sauces.
entries.summary: Cooked food that will be kept must lose its heat quickly, in two timed stages, so the bacteria that survive cooking never get the warm hours they need. Big, thick pots need the most help.
entries.guest: How the kitchen makes and keeps its soups and sauces is the chef's to answer, so let me ask and come straight back to you.

paras: Cooling is the stretch between the stove and the fridge, where big batches most often go wrong. Cooking kills most bacteria but not all: Clostridium perfringens and Bacillus cereus form spores, tough resting cells that survive the boil and wake as the food cools. In a deep pot that cools slowly they multiply through the warm hours, and a stock or a pot of beans that looked fine can make a dining room ill.

The FDA Food Code, the model behind most American health codes, calls such foods TCS, short for time and temperature control for safety: stocks, sauces, soups, cooked rice, beans and meat. Cooling is a clock nobody can see on the plate, so it is timed, probed and written down.

The Food Code sets two stages. First, from 57°C (135°F) to 21°C (70°F) within 2 hours. Then on to 5°C (41°F) or below within a total of 6 hours, so if the first stage takes its full 2 hours, 4 hours remain for the second. The first stage has the shorter clock because it covers the range where bacteria grow quickest. These figures are the 2022 Food Code's; FDA issued a new edition on 17 September 2026 that adds an alternative cooling process, and the kitchen follows its own health authority's code and its written procedure.

Heat leaves through surfaces, so every tool gives the food more surface or more cold. Stand the pot in an ice bath, ice and water up to the level of the food, and stir: stirring carries hot liquid from the middle to the cold wall. An ice wand, a sealed paddle of frozen water, is stirred through the pot. Pour thick food into shallow metal pans, about 5 cm (2 inches) deep, and divide big batches. A blast chiller does the same work with fast, cold air, and where the recipe allows, ice can stand in for some of the water.

In the walk-in, cooling pans sit uncovered or loosely covered on a top shelf, with air around them and nothing stacked on top; a tight lid traps the heat. Probe the centre about every hour, so a slow pan is caught in time, and log each reading with its time. If the food is still above 21°C (70°F) at 2 hours, tell the chef at once; the written procedure decides whether it is reheated and cooled again or discarded.

Thin stock cools fastest because it circulates, carrying heat to the cold wall. Thick food barely moves, so heat has to creep out through the food itself. Gumbo, roux-thickened sauces such as velouté and espagnole, red beans, rice and braises can keep a warm core for hours in a deep pot. They need the most care: shallow pans at once, frequent stirring and the probe in the centre, never at the edge.

Never put a full, hot stockpot straight into the walk-in. A walk-in holds cold food cold; it is not built to pull the heat out of 20 litres (about 5 gallons) of stock. The pot warms the air and everything near it, the cream and the raw fish included, while its own centre stays warm far into the night.

Cooled food wanted hot again is reheated quickly on the stove or in the oven, never in the steam table, until every part reaches 74°C (165°F) for 15 seconds, within 2 hours. Every container in the walk-in is labelled with what it is, the date and time it was made and the cook's initials. Ready-to-eat food kept longer than 24 hours is also marked with its last day, at most 7 days at 5°C (41°F) or below, with the day of making counted as the first.

Most cooling failures are quiet: a pot left on the range to cool a little loses its first hour, a lid traps the heat, the ice melts unnoticed, a warm core goes unprobed. A stock that smells sour or looks cloudy and fizzy has cooled too slowly or been kept too long. It is thrown away, never boiled again in hope: boiling does not undo the toxins some bacteria have already made.

A server never sees the cooling, but its questions reach the table: was the soup made today, has it been reheated? Never guess; take the question to the kitchen. Out front, a lukewarm soup goes back, and an unlabelled container in a side station goes to the chef.

entries.title: The danger zone and hot holding
entries.say: As it reads: the danger zone and hot holding.
entries.summary: The danger zone is 5 to 57°C (41 to 135°F), where bacteria multiply fastest. Food is held above or below it, checked with a calibrated thermometer, or kept on a written clock and served or thrown away by its marked time.
entries.guest: Hot dishes go out hot and cold dishes cold; if anything reaches you lukewarm, please tell me and I will take it straight back to the kitchen.

paras: The danger zone is the band of temperatures in which the bacteria that make people ill multiply fastest. The FDA Food Code, the model behind most American health codes, sets its edges through its holding rules: 5 to 57°C (41 to 135°F). Cold below it slows most bacteria to a crawl; heat above it stops them growing. The USDA notes that in its own, slightly wider band bacteria can double in number in as little as 20 minutes, so a pan left out all afternoon can turn a few hundred cells into millions.

The Food Code figures in this entry come from its 2022 edition; FDA issued a new edition on 17 September 2026, and a kitchen works to the code its own authority has adopted, so learn the house's numbers. The rule is simple: food is kept hot, kept cold or kept on a written clock, and it passes through the zone as quickly as it can.

Hot holding means cooked food kept at 57°C (135°F) or above until it is served; cold holding means 5°C (41°F) or below. Steam tables, bains-marie (pans of hot water in which containers of sauce stand to keep warm), soup wells and warming drawers hold hot food; the fridge, the walk-in and the cold rail, the chilled well of containers on the line, hold cold. Keep lids on, stir soups and sauces so the top does not cool, keep the water topped up, and take the food's own temperature: the unit's dial reads the water or the air, not the sauce.

Steam tables and bains-marie hold heat; they are not built to raise it. Cooled food set in a steam table climbs through the zone far too slowly, so it is reheated first, on the stove or in the oven, until every part reaches 74°C (165°F). The cold side works the same way: a cold rail keeps chilled food cold, it does not chill warm food.

Use the thermometer every time: stir, push the probe into the thickest part or the centre of the pan, wait for the reading to settle and write it on the log. Clean and sanitise the probe between foods so it never carries raw juices into cooked food. Calibrate it at the start of each shift and after any knock: in a glass packed with crushed ice and topped with water, it should read the freezing point of water; if not, adjust it or take it out of use. The Food Code asks for accuracy within one degree Celsius, or two Fahrenheit.

Some kitchens use a written exception called time as a public health control: instead of holding a food hot or cold, they hold it on a clock. Under the Food Code the food starts at 5°C (41°F) or below, or at 57°C (135°F) or above, and is marked with the time 4 hours after it left temperature control. Within those 4 hours it is served or thrown away. It never goes back into the fridge or the hot well to reset the clock, and an unmarked container is discarded.

A second form allows up to 6 hours for cold food that starts at 5°C (41°F) or below and never rises above 21°C (70°F). Either way the procedure is written in advance, kept in the kitchen and shown to the health inspector on request, and the cook follows it, not memory.

Holding fails in small, ordinary ways: a soup well with its water run dry, a sauce judged by the dial, a pan left on the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, between rushes, a thermometer not calibrated since it fell, a cold rail packed above its fill line so the top layer sits in warm air. Each has the same cure, a probe in the food and a reading on the log, and a wrong reading goes straight to the chef.

Servers hold food too: at the pass, at the tray stand, a folding rack for a loaded tray, and at the side station, the servers' stand in the dining room. Run plates as soon as they are up, keep cold garnishes and butter in the cold, and never park a plate under a heat lamp for a table that is not ready. A guest who says a dish is lukewarm is thanked, and the plate goes back to the kitchen for the chef to decide.

entries.title: Cooking temperatures and the consumer advisory
entries.say: As it reads: cooking temperatures and the consumer advisory.
entries.summary: Learn the difference between a cooking target and a reliable measurement: identify the food and required holding time, position the thermometer correctly and verify the result. Follow the local code and the kitchen’s written procedure.
entries.guest: How would you like your steak cooked? The note on the menu covers raw and undercooked dishes, and I am glad to take any question about it to the chef.

paras: Cooking kills the bacteria raw animal food carries, by temperature and time together: the hotter the food, the shorter the hold it needs. The FDA Food Code sets each food a minimum internal temperature and a time to hold it there. Poultry, and stuffed meat, fish and pasta, go to 74°C (165°F) for an instant, less than 1 second. Minced meat goes to 68°C (155°F) for 17 seconds. Fish and whole cuts of meat, such as steaks and chops, go to 63°C (145°F) for 15 seconds.

Minced meat illustrates time and temperature together: the 2022 code also accepts 63°C (145°F) for 3 minutes, 66°C (150°F) for 1 minute or 70°C (158°F) for an instant. FDA issued the 2026 edition on 17 September 2026. Follow the locally adopted code and the kitchen’s written standard; home-cooking guidance differs.

Choose a suitable probe and follow its maker’s insertion-depth and response-time instructions. Centre the sensing area in the thickest part, avoiding bone, fat, gristle and the pan. Enter thin food from the side. Check each piece and several locations on irregular food; colour cannot verify internal temperature.

Carryover is the variable rise in internal temperature after cooking. Never assume it completes a required cooking step or invent an early-pull target. Professional kitchens must verify their approved process’s temperature and holding time. USDA home guidance requires the listed minimum before removal from heat, followed by any stated rest; that consumer chart is separate from the Food Code figures above.

Before and after use, wash, rinse, sanitise and air-dry the food-contact stem following equipment and kitchen instructions. Protect electronics unless designed for immersion. Check accuracy regularly and after a knock; adjust only as permitted, otherwise remove an inaccurate instrument from service.

The Food Code has a specific exception for whole-muscle, intact beef steak; it is not a promise that every whole cut has a sterile centre. The steak must be identified as intact by its supplier, must not be served to a highly susceptible population, and must reach at least 63°C (145°F) on top and bottom with a cooked colour change on all external surfaces. Needle-tenderised, injected and minced meats are not covered by that intact-steak exception.

Mincing spreads the surface through the whole batch, and a needle-tenderised or injected steak has had its surface pushed inside, so their centres must be cooked. Stuffing soaks up raw juices and sits at the coolest heart of the dish, which is why stuffed foods take the poultry figure.

Some dishes are raw or undercooked by design: steak tartare, a rosy duck breast, an egg with a runny yolk, oysters on the half shell. The code allows them when the guest asks for or chooses them, outside places that serve highly susceptible groups, provided the guest is told through the consumer advisory, and never undercooked minced meat from a children's menu.

The advisory has two parts. The disclosure marks the dish, with a plain description such as oysters on the half shell (raw oysters) or an asterisk to a footnote saying it is served raw or undercooked. The reminder is the warning, in words such as: consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness, and the kitchen answers any question it raises. It matters most to young children, older people, anyone pregnant and anyone whose immune system is weakened.

Three Brennan's dishes show the rules. The Steak Tartare Cannoli is raw beef tartare in a crisp potato shell with a grated cured egg yolk, and its service note marks it for the consumer advisory. The Roasted Rohan Duck Breast on the dinner tasting is served rosy, usually medium-rare to medium: confirm the kitchen's standard at lineup. Whether our menu marks the duck for the advisory is confirmed at lineup too. The Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is at its best medium-rare to medium; always ask the temperature and write it on the ticket.

At the table, ask the doneness of every steak, duck breast and burger, and write it on the ticket. If a guest asks whether rare or raw is risky, neither reassure nor frighten: point to the note on the menu, say the chef can answer, and bring the answer back. Never promise an outcome, and never change the doneness a guest chose without asking.

entries.title: Shellfish handling
entries.summary: How a kitchen keeps crab, crawfish and shrimp fit to serve: live ones cool, damp and lively, picked meat and tails cold, frozen shrimp thawed the right way, raw kept apart from cooked, and the allergen carried in shells, stock and fryer oil.
entries.guest: Our crab claws are served warm, in a brown butter vinaigrette, so here are napkins and a plate for the shells. Any question about the crab or crawfish, I will take to the chef.

paras: Shellfish, in a kitchen's language, comes in two families: crustaceans, with jointed shells and legs, such as crab, crawfish and shrimp, and molluscs, such as oysters and clams. This entry is about the crustaceans; raw oysters have their own entry. Crab and crawfish flesh breaks down quickly once the animal dies, so the habits are strict: live animals kept alive until cooked, cooked meat kept cold and clean, raw always apart from ready to eat.

A crab or crawfish that died before cooking may already be spoiling, and boiling cannot make it good again. And crustacean shellfish is a major food allergen, so a careless board, stock or fryer can harm a guest who never ordered crab; the kitchen guards against both.

Live crawfish and blue crabs go straight from their ventilated sacks to somewhere cool and damp: the walk-in, or a cooler with the animals kept above the meltwater, under wet sacking. Never seal them in plastic, and never leave them in a tub of still water or melted ice, where they use up the oxygen and die. Before cooking, rinse crawfish in clean running water and sort every batch: lively ones move their legs and claws when handled. Any that are limp and still, or smell off, are dead and go in the bin, never in the pot.

Fresh shrimp and picked crabmeat are held at 5°C (41°F) or below, the Food Code's cold-holding figure, on ice that drains or in the walk-in, and used by the date on the container. Frozen shrimp thaw in the walk-in overnight, or sealed and fully under cold running water no warmer than 21°C (70°F); never on the bench or in warm water. Under running water, raw seafood may spend no more than 4 hours above 5°C (41°F), counting the thaw and the preparation before cooking. A vacuum pack of frozen seafood labelled keep frozen is opened before it thaws in the walk-in, because without air the bacteria behind botulism can grow.

Raw shellfish gets its own boards, knives, gloves and trays in the kitchen, and its own shelf in the walk-in: below cooked and ready-to-eat food, and above raw meat and poultry, which need hotter cooking, so nothing drips onto food that will be cooked less or not at all. Many kitchens colour-code boards, often blue for raw seafood; follow the house chart. Wash hands and change gloves between raw and cooked, and wash, rinse and sanitise a board before it changes job.

Cooked crab claws and lump crabmeat are ready to eat: warmed, never cooked again, so whatever touches them reaches the guest. Handle them with gloves or tongs, never bare hands, keep them cold until warmed, pick lump meat over gently for shell on a clean board, and warm only what has been ordered.

Crustacean shellfish is one of the nine major food allergens in the United States, and the protein runs through the whole animal, so the kitchen treats shells, heads, cooking water and stock as carriers too. Shrimp-shell stock in a sauce, crawfish fat in a filling, or fries cooked in oil that fried popcorn shrimp can each reach a guest who ordered none. Cooking does not destroy the allergen, however long the kitchen boils it. Molluscs such as oysters and clams are not on the federal list, but some guests react to them too, so every shellfish question goes to the kitchen.

At Brennan's the Louisiana Crab Claws arrive already cooked and chilled, so the kitchen only warms them through; cooking them again tightens the meat onto the cartilage. The lump crab on the Pecan Gulf Fish is treated the same way: warmed gently, never cooked again. The Crawfish Meat Pies on the Bubbles list are filled with crawfish; how the filling is made is not printed, so ask before describing it.

Describe the claws as served warm, so nobody expects a cold cocktail claw, and bring napkins and a plate for the shells. Where the crab or crawfish come from, how they are cooked, or whether the claws can come chilled are questions for the chef: never guess a supplier or an origin. When a guest mentions a shellfish allergy, stop selling, write it on the ticket and take it to the kitchen, as the allergen conversation entry teaches.

cards.front: How are live crawfish and blue crabs kept before cooking?
cards.back: Cool and damp, in a ventilated sack under wet sacking, never sealed in plastic and never in still water or meltwater, where they use up the oxygen and die.

cards.front: What happens to a crab or crawfish that is dead before cooking?
cards.back: It is thrown away. The flesh begins to spoil quickly after death, and boiling cannot make spoiled meat good again.

cards.front: At what temperature are fresh shrimp and picked crabmeat held?
cards.back: At 5°C (41°F) or below, on ice that drains or in the walk-in, and used by the date on the container.

cards.front: What are the two everyday ways to thaw frozen shrimp?
cards.back: In the walk-in overnight, or sealed and fully under cold running water no warmer than 21°C (70°F); never on the bench or in warm water.

cards.front: Thawed under running water, how long may raw seafood spend above 5°C (41°F)?
cards.back: No more than 4 hours under the Food Code, counting both the thaw and the preparation before cooking.

cards.front: Why is a vacuum pack of frozen seafood labelled keep frozen opened before it thaws in the walk-in?
cards.back: Without air, the bacteria behind botulism can grow as the fish warms, so the Food Code asks for the pack to be opened before it thaws.

cards.front: How does a kitchen keep raw shellfish apart from cooked food?
cards.back: Its own boards, knives, gloves and trays, a shelf below ready-to-eat food and above raw meat and poultry, and hands washed between raw and cooked.

cards.front: Why are cooked crab claws and lump crabmeat handled with gloves or tongs?
cards.back: They are ready to eat, only warmed and never cooked again, so anything a bare hand leaves on them reaches the guest.

cards.front: Besides the meat, where can the crustacean allergen hide in a kitchen?
cards.back: In shells, heads, cooking water, stock, crawfish fat and fryer oil. Cooking does not destroy it, so every one of them counts.

cards.front: Why does a shellfish allergy question about the oysters still go to the kitchen?
cards.back: Molluscs such as oysters and clams are not on the federal list, but some guests react to them as well as to crab, so the kitchen answers every time.

cards.front: How does the Brennan's kitchen treat the Louisiana Crab Claws?
cards.back: They arrive already cooked and chilled, so they are only warmed through; cooking again tightens the meat onto the cartilage. Say served warm.

cards.front: A guest asks where tonight's crawfish come from. What does a server say?
cards.back: Only what the menu prints, then that the chef will tell us; a server never guesses an origin or a supplier.

questions.q: A delivery of live crawfish arrives. How should it be kept until cooking?
questions.answer: Cool and damp, in its sack under wet sacking
distractors: Sunk in a tub of fresh water to keep clean
Sealed in a lidded tub in the walk-in
Packed in ice with the meltwater left to pool
questions.why: Crawfish need air and cool damp: still water uses up the oxygen and drowns them, sealing suffocates them, and warmth spoils them.

questions.q: Sorting crabs before the boil, a cook finds one limp and still. What happens to it?
questions.answer: It is thrown away
distractors: It is boiled longer than the rest
It is picked first for crabmeat
It is chilled and cooked tomorrow
questions.why: A crab that died before cooking may already be spoiling, and no amount of boiling makes spoiled meat good again.

questions.q: Picked crabmeat arrives on ice that has turned to standing meltwater. What does the cook do?
questions.answer: Drain it and re-ice it, or move it to the walk-in
distractors: Leave it, since the meltwater is still cold
Top up the meltwater with fresh ice
Rinse the crabmeat in the meltwater
questions.why: Picked crabmeat is held at 5°C (41°F) or below, on ice that drains or in the walk-in; standing meltwater warms and soaks the meat.

questions.q: Which is a correct way to thaw a frozen block of shrimp for tonight's service?
questions.answer: Sealed and fully under cold running water
distractors: In a sink of cold water, left to stand
On the bench for the afternoon
In the microwave, then held for tomorrow
questions.why: Shrimp thaw in the walk-in or sealed under running water no warmer than 21°C (70°F); standing water warms up, the bench is warm, and microwaved shrimp must be cooked at once.

questions.q: Where does a box of raw shrimp go in the walk-in?
questions.answer: Below ready-to-eat food, above raw meat and poultry
distractors: On the top shelf, above the desserts
Beside the cooked claws, to save space
On the bottom shelf, under the raw chicken
questions.why: Raw seafood sits below ready-to-eat food and above raw meat and poultry, so nothing drips onto food that will be cooked less hot or not at all.

questions.q: Why must lump crabmeat never be handled with bare hands?
questions.answer: It is ready to eat and will only be warmed
distractors: It is raw and will be cooked through later
Body heat would start to cook it
The bare-hand rule covers raw seafood only
questions.why: Lump crabmeat arrives cooked and is only warmed, so nothing kills what a bare hand leaves on it before it reaches the guest.

questions.q: For a crustacean allergy flagged to the kitchen, which sauce base carries crustacean protein even after it is strained?
questions.answer: A stock made from crab shells
distractors: A fish fumet made from redfish bones
A stock made from oyster liquor
A vegetable stock of the holy trinity
questions.why: Crustacean protein runs through shells and survives straining and cooking, so a crab-shell stock carries it; fish and oysters belong to other families, and every question still goes to the kitchen.

questions.q: A guest allergic to shellfish says the oysters must be all right, since they are not crab or shrimp, so there is no need to ask the kitchen. What do you do?
questions.answer: Write it on the ticket and ask the kitchen
distractors: Say yes: oysters are not on the federal list
Say no: every seafood dish is off limits
Offer the cooked oysters instead of the raw
questions.why: Molluscs such as oysters are not on the federal list, but some guests with a shellfish allergy react to them, so the kitchen answers every time.

questions.q: Why does the Brennan's kitchen only warm the Louisiana Crab Claws through?
questions.answer: They arrive cooked, and more heat tightens the meat
distractors: They are served chilled, like a cocktail claw
The guest finishes them at the table
They are poached raw to order in butter
questions.why: The claws come already cooked and chilled; cooking them again tightens the meat onto the cartilage and makes it hard to pull.

entries.title: Flambé safety at the table
entries.say: As it reads: flambé, flahm-BAY, safety at the table.
entries.summary: The habits that keep a flame at the table a show and never a fire: the spirit measured first, the pan off the flame when it goes in, clear space around the cart, a lid in reach and the burner off before leaving.
entries.guest: We flame this right here at the table, so may I ask everyone to sit back a little while I light it? The flame dies down on its own.

paras: Flambé (flahm-BAY) means flamed: spirit poured into a hot pan and lit, so that its alcohol vapour burns above the sauce. At the table it happens on a guéridon (gay-ree-DOHN), a wheeled cart with a burner, beside guests in a full room. The cook is handling an open flame, a pan of hot butter and sugar, and a spirit that burns, among tablecloths, sleeves and children. Every rule below exists because one of those can meet another. The method and the dish build have their own entries; this one keeps everyone unhurt.

Set the cart before anything is lit. It stands where nothing hangs overhead, no drapes, garlands, low beams or decorations, and away from air vents and draughts that push a flame sideways. Clear menus, napkins and paper from its top. Check the burner and its fuel, and keep spare fuel out of the dining room. Tie back long hair and fasten loose sleeves. Seat the guests and ask them to sit back; nobody leans in, and children are watched.

Measure the spirit into a small vessel before you begin, exactly what the house recipe calls for, and keep the bottle off the cart. Never pour from the bottle near a flame: vapour at the neck can catch, and the flame can run back into the bottle. Never add spirit to a pan that is alight, or might be. Never swap in a stronger spirit than the one you trained with; it flares higher and faster.

Pull the pan off the flame and pour in the measured spirit. Return it to the burner and tilt the far edge down towards the flame, so the vapour catches on the side away from you and the guests. Keep your face and arms back, because the flame climbs higher than you expect. Hold the pan steady, let the flame burn out on its own, and never carry a pan while it is alight.

For a small fire contained in the pan, slide a suitable metal lid over it and turn off the heat if you can do so without approaching the flame. Leave the pan in place and keep it covered until cool. Do not use water or an improvised wet cloth. If fire spreads or you cannot control it, move people away and follow the house emergency plan, including calling the fire service. Know the extinguisher location and use it only within your training. An alcohol flame can be hard to see in bright light, so never test for it with a hand or cloth.

At Brennan's two desserts are flamed at the table, the World Famous Bananas Foster and the Cherries Jubilee, though the Jubilee was not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026, so a manager confirms it is served before it is offered. The Jubilee follows the Foster's safety steps, and the kitchen says whether its cherries are pitted, so guests can be warned if not. A new server does not light a pan before sign off.

The Foster's service note sets out the safety steps to learn word for word: the cart clear of anything overhead, drapes, décor and air vents; guests seated and back; the rum measured first; the pan off the flame to add it, then tilted away to ignite; never alcohol into a lit pan; a lid in reach and the extinguisher known; the flame burnt out before plating, and the burner off before leaving.

Before the spirit goes in, give the table a cue, please sit back a little, then stop talking and watch the pan: talk draws eyes and hands towards it. Pour any wine before the flame, so no glass stands near it. If a guest asks whether the flame burns off the alcohol, be exact: it burns the vapour, and alcohol can remain in the sauce, which a guest who avoids alcohol hears before ordering. If anything feels wrong, a draught, a crowded table, a child too close, pause and fetch a manager.

faults.fault: Spirit poured from the bottle over the pan
faults.cause: Hurry, or no measure set out before the cart rolled.
faults.fix: Measure into a small vessel before you begin and keep the bottle off the cart.

faults.fault: The flame will not catch, so more spirit goes in
faults.cause: The pan cooled, or the spirit was too cold.
faults.fix: Warm the pan and tilt again; never add spirit to a pan that may be alight.

faults.fault: The flame leans towards a guest
faults.cause: The cart stands under an air vent or in a draught, or the pan was tilted towards the table.
faults.fix: Move the cart before you start, and tilt the far edge to the burner, away from the guests.

faults.fault: A sleeve or a napkin catches
faults.cause: Loose cuffs, paper left on the cart, or a guest leaning in.
faults.fix: Clear the cart, fasten sleeves and seat the guests back before the spirit goes in.

faults.fault: The cart left with the burner on
faults.cause: Distracted by plating or by another table.
faults.fix: Burner off is the last step before you leave the cart, every time.

brennans.how: The Bananas Foster is flamed with rum on the guéridon. Its service note lists the steps: rum measured first, the pan off the flame to add it, tilted away to ignite, a lid in reach, the burner off before leaving.

The Cherries Jubilee is flamed at the table under the Foster's safety steps. It was not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026, so confirm with a manager that it is served, and ask the kitchen whether the cherries are pitted.

cards.front: Why is the spirit measured into a small vessel before a flambé?
cards.back: So the bottle never comes near the flame: vapour at the neck can catch, and the flame can run back into the bottle.

cards.front: At what moment does the spirit go into the pan?
cards.back: With the pan pulled off the flame. Then it goes back to the burner, and the far edge is tilted down to ignite.

cards.front: Which way does the pan tilt to light the spirit?
cards.back: The far edge towards the burner, so the flame rises on the side away from the cook and the guests.

cards.front: The flame will not catch. May you add more spirit?
cards.back: Never into a pan that is, or may be, alight: a stream of spirit can carry the flame back to the vessel. Warm the pan and tilt again.

cards.front: Where should the guéridon stand for a flambé?
cards.back: Where nothing hangs overhead, away from drapes, decorations, low ceilings and air vents, with menus, napkins and paper cleared from its top.

cards.front: What does the cook check about people before lighting the pan?
cards.back: Long hair tied back, sleeves fastened, guests seated and sitting back, nobody leaning in, and children watched.

cards.front: What must be within reach throughout a flambé?
cards.back: A suitable metal lid for a small fire contained in the pan. Know the extinguisher location and the house emergency plan; a spreading fire requires evacuation and emergency help.

cards.front: Why is water never thrown on a flaming flambé pan?
cards.back: Water can scatter burning fat. For a small contained fire, cover the pan and turn off the heat if you can do so without approaching the flame; do not move it.

cards.front: Why treat the pan as lit even when you can see no flame?
cards.back: In a bright room an alcohol flame can be almost invisible, a pale shimmer; never pass a hand or a cloth over it to check.

cards.front: What is the last step before the cook leaves the cart?
cards.back: Turn the burner off, every time, once the flame has died and the dessert is plated.

cards.front: Which Brennan's desserts are flamed at the table, and whose safety steps apply?
cards.back: The Bananas Foster, and the Cherries Jubilee once a manager confirms it is served; the Jubilee follows the same steps as the Foster's service note.

cards.front: Does the flame burn off all the alcohol in a flambé?
cards.back: No. It burns the vapour above the pan, and alcohol can remain in the sauce; tell a guest who avoids it before ordering.

questions.q: Why must spirit never be poured straight from the bottle near a flame?
questions.answer: Flame can travel back into the bottle
distractors: The spirit loses its flavour
The pour is too slow for service
The bottle's label may scorch
questions.why: Vapour at the neck can catch, and the flame can run back into the bottle; a small measured vessel keeps the bottle away from the burner.

questions.q: At which moment does the measured spirit go into the pan?
questions.answer: With the pan pulled off the flame
distractors: While the pan sits over full flame
After the flame is already burning
Once the dessert is on the plate
questions.why: Off the flame the spirit cannot catch as it is poured; the pan then goes back and is tilted so the vapour lights under control.

questions.q: To light the spirit, which way does the cook tilt the pan?
questions.answer: Far edge to the burner, away from people
distractors: Near edge towards the cook's face
Towards the guests, so they see it
Level, with a lighter held over it
questions.why: Tilting the far edge to the burner lights the vapour on the side away from the cook and the table, so the flame rises away from people.

questions.q: The rum has not caught. What should the cook never do next?
questions.answer: Pour more spirit into the pan
distractors: Warm the pan a little longer
Tilt the far edge to the burner again
Check that the burner is lit
questions.why: A pan that seems unlit may be burning invisibly, and a stream of spirit can carry the flame back to the vessel in the cook's hand.

questions.q: Which place is right for the guéridon during a flambé?
questions.answer: Clear of drapes and vents, with nothing overhead
distractors: Under the chandelier for the best light
Beside the curtains, out of the way
Below an air vent, to carry smoke off
questions.why: Flame climbs higher than expected and a draught pushes it sideways, so the cart stands where nothing hangs above it and no vent blows across it.

questions.q: A small fire is contained in the pan. You can reach the controls without approaching it. What is the first response?
questions.answer: Cover the pan and turn the heat off
distractors: Throw a glass of water over it
Carry the pan quickly to the kitchen
Blow hard across the top of the pan
questions.why: A suitable lid covers a small contained pan fire. Leave it in place until cool; if fire spreads or cannot be controlled, follow the house emergency plan.

questions.q: In a sunny breakfast room you can see no flame on the pan. What do you assume?
questions.answer: The pan may still be lit
distractors: The flame has certainly died
The spirit never caught
The burner has gone out
questions.why: An alcohol flame can be almost invisible in bright light, so the pan is treated as lit until it has clearly died.

questions.q: What is the last thing a cook does before leaving the cart?
questions.answer: Turns the burner off
distractors: Tops up the spirit vessel
Leaves the pan warming
Lights the next pan
questions.why: A burner left on beside a full room is a fire waiting for a napkin or a sleeve, so turning it off is always the last step.

questions.q: A guest who avoids alcohol asks whether the flame burns it all off. What is true?
questions.answer: Alcohol can remain after flaming
distractors: All of it burns away in the flame
Only the sugar burns, never the spirit
It burns off once the ice cream melts
questions.why: The flame burns the vapour above the pan, not the whole spirit, so a guest who avoids alcohol hears this before ordering and chooses for themselves.

entries.title: Cross-contact and the allergen conversation
entries.say: As it reads: cross-contact and the allergen conversation.
entries.summary: What every server and cook must know: the nine major food allergens the law names, how cross-contact carries them onto a plate that never listed them, where they hide on a Creole menu, and the routine that takes every question to the kitchen.
entries.guest: Thank you for telling me. I am writing it on the ticket and taking it to the chef myself, and I will come back with what the kitchen can make for you.

paras: To the kitchen, a food allergy is the body's immune system reacting to a protein in a food, and for some guests a trace is enough to cause a severe reaction, even one that threatens life. An intolerance or a diet is different, but the kitchen treats every such question with the same care. US law names nine major food allergens, and every kitchen learns them by heart: milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soy and sesame. The first eight were named by a law of 2004, and sesame joined them on 1 January 2023, so a kitchen's older charts may show only eight.

Cross-contact is the kitchen's word for an allergen moving from one food to another by a shared fryer, board, knife, pan, glove, spoon or garnish, so that a dish carries it though no recipe lists it. Kitchens keep the word cross-contamination for bacteria, and the difference matters: cooking kills most bacteria but does not destroy an allergen, so a hot fryer or a long simmer never makes a shared pan clean. Only a thorough wash does, and fryer oil cannot be washed, which is why a shared fryer is a question for the kitchen every time.

On a Creole menu the allergens often hide in the kitchen's foundations, and every one of them is a question for the kitchen. A roux is flour cooked in fat, so a gumbo, a turtle soup or a roux-bound sauce is usually built on wheat that no menu line names. Butter is milk, and it is everywhere: in blackening, where food is classically dipped in melted butter before the spice, and in beurre blanc, hollandaise, a meunière (fish finished with browned butter and lemon) and New Orleans barbecue sauce.

Pecans, a tree nut, turn up in sauces, crumbles and pralines, and the kitchen knows where. Stock made from shrimp shells or crab carries crustacean shellfish into rice, sauces and soups, which only the kitchen can trace. Worcestershire sauce is traditionally made with anchovy, which is fish, and it goes into barbecue butter, dressings and Bloody Marys.

The server's routine is the same every time. Listen: let the guest say it in full, and neither argue nor reassure. Write it on the ticket, against the right seat. Tell the kitchen in person, the chef or whoever runs the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, not only through the printer: a ticket can be missed in a rush, a face rarely is. Bring back the chef's answer in the chef's words.

When the plate is ready, carry it separately, by itself, straight from the pass to the guest, so nothing drips or brushes onto it on the way, and name it as it lands. If a guest shows any sign of a reaction, fetch the manager at once and call for emergency help; never wait to see.

No verdict ever comes from the floor. A server never promises that a dish is without an allergen, never says it should be fine and never guesses from the menu, because only the kitchen knows every ingredient, every pan and every change of supplier. The kitchen confirms every time, even for a dish the guest ate last week. Diet questions take the same road to the kitchen: vegan or vegetarian, gluten, gelatine in a set dessert such as a Bavarian cream, and alcohol in a sauce or a flamed dessert, where flaming does not guarantee an alcohol-free result.

At Brennan's the house rule is plain: guests are asked to note their needs at the reservation, the server writes them on the ticket and tells the captain, the senior server who runs the section, and the kitchen, not the server, says what a dish can do. Blackening is traditionally done with butter, so the Blackened Tofu is never called vegan: the server asks the kitchen each time a guest asks, as the service note says, and asks too whether the rice grits use any stock.

The Seafood Gumbo is usually built on a roux, so gluten questions about it go to the kitchen. Pecans run through the menus, from the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish to the pralines on the bread pudding; nut questions go to the kitchen and the service note.

faults.fault: A server tells a guest a dish should be fine
faults.cause: Wanting to reassure, or reading the menu as if it listed every ingredient.
faults.fix: Say only what the menu prints, then take the question to the kitchen and bring back the chef's answer.

faults.fault: An allergy on the ticket that the kitchen never heard about
faults.cause: Trusting the printer alone in a rush.
faults.fix: Tell the chef in person as well, every time, and tell the captain.

faults.fault: A plate for an allergy, approved by the kitchen, carried on a full tray
faults.cause: Saving a trip.
faults.fix: Carry it alone, straight from the pass, and name it as it lands.

faults.fault: Fried food sent without a word about the oil
faults.cause: Thinking of the recipe and forgetting the fryer.
faults.fix: Ask the kitchen which fryer it went through; oil carries whatever was fried in it.

faults.fault: A garnish added after the kitchen approved the allergy plate
faults.cause: A finishing touch at the side station: nuts, a sauce, a piece of bread.
faults.fix: Nothing goes onto an approved plate without the chef's word.

brennans.how: Blackening is traditionally done with butter, so the Blackened Tofu is never called vegan; ask the kitchen each time, and ask whether the rice grits use any stock, as the service note says.

Gumbo is usually built on a roux, flour cooked in fat, so the Seafood Gumbo can carry wheat the menu line never names. Questions about flour, and about the shrimp, crab and oysters in it, go to the kitchen.
Pecans go into the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish, which also carries lump crab. Name the pecans and the crab as printed, and send every nut question to the kitchen and the service note.

questions.q: Which of these is not one of the nine major food allergens a US kitchen must know?

Milk

questions.q: A dish lists no peanuts but was garnished with a spoon just used for peanuts. What is this called?

Cross-seasoning
Mise en place

questions.q: Fries go into oil that has just fried shrimp. A guest with a crustacean allergy asks the kitchen about them: what is true?

questions.q: Which part of a classic gumbo carries wheat that the menu line never names?
questions.answer: The roux, flour cooked in fat

The okra, a pod that thickens the pot
The holy trinity of onion, celery and pepper

questions.q: Which everyday sauce is traditionally made with anchovy, so a question about fish reaches it?

steps.title: Hold hollandaise through service
steps.prompt: Put the stages of holding a batch of hollandaise through service in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Take the yolks from the fridge for a small batch timed to service, and note the time: the sauce's clock starts there
Make the hollandaise, then strain it into a clean, dry container, never one that held the last batch
Label it the moment it is filled, with the time it was made and the time it must be gone, then stand it in a bain-marie that steams but never bubbles, away from the flame
Through service, stir it now and then so no skin forms, and check it with a probe thermometer
Discard it when its time runs out, or sooner if it splits, skins or smells sour, and start the next batch clean
steps.distractor: Pour the fresh batch onto what is left of the old sauce, so nothing goes to waste
steps.why: The clock starts when the yolks leave the fridge, not when the sauce is finished, and sets the label. Where it sits below 57°C (135°F), the sauce runs on the kitchen's written time limit. Old sauce is never topped up: the new batch would take on its time and whatever has grown in it.

steps.title: Cool a stock in two stages
steps.prompt: Put the stages of cooling a large batch of stock in order, from the stove to the walk-in. One stage does not belong.
steps: Take the stock off the stove and start cooling at once, never leaving it on the range
Strain the stock off its bones and vegetables, dividing it among smaller metal containers
Stand them in an ice bath, with ice and water up to the level of the stock
Stir the stock often, or stir an ice wand through it, topping up the ice as it melts
Probe the centre of each and log it: down to 21°C (70°F) within 2 hours
Once it has reached 21°C (70°F), label each container and set it on a top shelf of the walk-in, loosely covered, with nothing stacked on it
Probe and log again: 5°C (41°F) or below within 6 hours of the start
steps.distractor: Put the full stockpot straight into the walk-in with a tight lid on
steps.why: Straining takes out the bones and vegetables that hold heat; the batch is divided and set in ice at once, and stirring carries heat to the cold wall. The first stage, to 21°C (70°F) within 2 hours, has the shorter clock because bacteria grow quickest there. A hot pot in the walk-in warms everything around it.

steps.title: Take an allergy to the kitchen
steps.prompt: A guest tells you of a food allergy: put the server's routine in order, from the table to the kitchen and back. One stage does not belong.
steps: Listen while the guest says it in full, neither arguing nor reassuring
Write it on the ticket, against the right seat
Tell the chef, or whoever runs the pass, in person as well as through the printer
Bring the chef's answer back to the guest in the chef's words
When the plate is up, carry it by itself, straight from the pass
Name the dish as it lands in front of the guest
steps.distractor: Tell the guest the dish should be fine, since the menu does not list it
steps.why: The guest is heard in full and the need is written against the seat, then said to the chef face to face, because a printed ticket can be missed in a rush. Only the chef's answer goes back to the table, and the plate travels alone so nothing touches it on the way.
